query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The time-dependent plastic deformation resistance of high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings is primarily governed by their coherent multilayer interfaces, which, in conjunction with intrinsic lattice distortions from high configurational entropy, strongly pin dislocations and elevate the activation energy for creep deformation compared to a homogeneous (monolithic) HEA coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating composed of alternating high-entropy alloy layers and engineered interfacial layers that maintain a coherent, misfit-stressed structure.
generation.intervention: Fabricate a multilayer HEA coating with deliberately controlled interfacial characteristics (e.g., alternating layers with slight lattice parameter differences) versus a monolithic HEA coating.
generation.conditions: Creep or constant-load deformation tests conducted at room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures under controlled stress conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent interfacial boundaries that generate back-stresses and disrupt dislocation line continuity, reinforced by the intrinsic lattice distortion typical of HEAs.
generation.mechanism: The multilayer architecture produces pronounced misfit stresses at interfaces that act as preferential dislocation pinning sites. This barrier effect increases the activation energy for dislocation nucleation and glide, thereby reducing the rate of time-dependent (creep) plastic deformation compared to coatings that lack such interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical stress and temperature conditions, multilayer HEA coatings will exhibit significantly lower creep strains and delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to homogeneous (monolithic) HEA coatings.
generation.baseline: A conventional monolithic HEA protective coating without engineered multilayer interfaces.
generation.boundary: The predicted behavior is expected under moderate stress and temperature conditions where the integrity of multilayer interfaces is maintained. At very high temperatures or extreme stress levels that cause interfacial degradation, the effect may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal interlayer thickness, compositional differences between layers, and the long-term stability of the coherent interfaces remain uncertain and could influence the extent of the dislocation pinning effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample groups: one with a multilayer HEA protective coating featuring engineered, coherent interfaces, and a control group with a homogeneous, monolithic HEA coating. Subject both groups to constant-load creep tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures where the interfaces remain intact. Monitor the evolution of creep strain and dislocation behavior over time using nanoindentation, TEM, and in-situ microscopy.
measurements: Dislocation density and propagation profiles (TEM images)
Interface integrity and lattice parameter mapping (via high-resolution microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer HEA coatings do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in creep strain or an increased threshold for dislocation motion (i.e., higher activation energy for plastic deformation) compared to the monolithic coatings under identical test conditions, the proposed hypothesis is falsified.

Temperature dependence of elastic and plastic deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy

Abstract: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. On the evolving nature of c/a ratio in a hexagonal close-packed epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys

Abstract: Activation of different slip systems in hexagonal close packed (h.c.p.) metals depends primarily on the c/a ratio, which is an intrinsic property that can be altered through alloying addition. In conventional h.c.p. alloys where there is no diffusion-less phase transformation and associated transformation volume change with deformation, the c/a ratio remains constant during deformation. In the present study, c/a ratio and transformation volume change of h.c.p. epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys (HEAs) were quantified as functions of alloy chemistry, friction stir processing and tensile deformation. The study revealed that while intrinsic c/a is dependent on alloying elements, c/a of epsilon in transformative HEAs changes with processing and deformation. This is attributed to transformation volume change induced dependence of h.c.p. lattice parameters on microstructure and stress state. Lower than ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c + a〉 slip and deformation twinning in epsilon phase of transformative HEAs.

Tensile deformation behavior of twist grain boundaries in CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy bicrystals

Abstract: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEA) are a class of materials that consist of multiple elemental species in similar concentrations. The use of elements in far from dilute concentrations introduces a multi-dimensional composition design space by which the properties of metallic systems can be tailored. While the mechanical behavior of HEAs has been the subject of active research recently, the role of grain boundaries (GBs) in their deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Motivated by recent experiments on HEAs demonstrating that GBs act as nucleation sites for deformation twins, herein, we leverage atomistic simulations to construct a series of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA bicrystals with ⟨110⟩ and ⟨111⟩ symmetric twist GBs and examine their tensile behavior and underlying deformation mechanisms at 77 K. Simulation results reveal that plastic deformation proceeds by the nucleation of partial dislocations from GBs, which then grow with further loading by bowing into the bulk crystals leaving behind stacking faults.
